title: Public Citizen v. U.S. Department of Justice (1989)
summary: The Federal Advisory Committee Act does not apply to the Justice Department's confidential consultation of the ABA's judicial-nominee committee, because a literal reading of "utilized" would sweep absurdly wide, the legislative history points the other way, and reading the statute to cover the committee would raise serious Article II questions the Court avoids.
notes: Supreme Court of the United States, 1989. Key line: "Hence, we are loath to conclude that Congress intended to press ahead into dangerous constitutional thickets in the absence of firm evidence that it courted those perils." (Justice Brennan)

sections.Parties: The appellants were Public Citizen and the Washington Legal Foundation, two public-interest groups seeking access to the work of the American Bar Association's Standing Committee on Federal Judiciary. The appellee was the United States Department of Justice, which since 1952 has asked the ABA Committee for confidential evaluations of potential federal judicial nominees. The ABA Committee is a 14-member body of a private association of about 343,000 lawyers; it receives no federal funds and does not propose judges on its own initiative. It was not itself a party by the time the case reached the Supreme Court.
sections.Material Facts: Before announcing nominees for the courts of appeals, district courts and Court of International Trade, the President through the Justice Department sends a potential nominee an ABA questionnaire. A committee member investigates, interviews judges and lawyers, and recommends a rating of exceptionally well qualified, well qualified, qualified or not qualified. The chair reports informally and in confidence to the Attorney General's office; if a formal report is requested the full committee votes and conveys its rating, but not its report, in confidence. Only after nomination is the rating made public. FACA defines "advisory committee" as any committee "established or utilized" by the President or an agency to obtain advice, and requires covered committees to file a charter, keep minutes, give notice and open their meetings. The ABA Committee refused WLF's request for the names of candidates it was considering and for its reports and minutes.
sections.Procedural History: In October 1986 the Washington Legal Foundation sued the Justice Department in the United States District Court for the District of Columbia, seeking a declaration that the ABA Committee is an advisory committee under FACA and an injunction barring the Department from using it until it complied. Public Citizen intervened as a plaintiff. The Department moved to dismiss. The district court dismissed, holding that FACA covered the Department's use of the ABA Committee but that applying it would unconstitutionally infringe the President's Article II nomination power. 691 F. Supp. 483 (1988). The Supreme Court noted probable jurisdiction on direct appeal and affirmed on statutory grounds, holding that FACA does not apply and declining to reach the constitutional questions.
sections.Issue: Whether the ABA Standing Committee on Federal Judiciary is an "advisory committee" under section 3(2) of the Federal Advisory Committee Act, which covers any committee "established or utilized" by the President or an agency to obtain advice, when the Justice Department concededly did not establish the committee but does make regular use of its confidential ratings of potential judicial nominees.
sections.Holding: No. Although the Executive "utilizes" the ABA Committee in one common sense of the word, Congress did not intend "utilized" to bear that unqualified meaning. FACA's purposes, its predecessor Executive Order 11007, and the origin of the phrase "or utilized" in the Conference Committee show that Congress meant to reach committees formed directly or indirectly by or for the government, not private groups whose views the government solicits. Because the question is close and the broader reading would raise serious separation-of-powers questions about the President's nomination power, the Court adopts the narrower construction. The judgment is affirmed.
sections.Reasoning: Brennan conceded that the Department makes use of the ABA Committee, so a straightforward reading of "utilize" covers it. But "utilize" is a woolly verb, and read unqualifiedly it would impose charters, federal chairs and open meetings on any consultation with the NAACP before an EEOC nomination, an American Legion post, or the President's own party before choosing a Cabinet. Congress could not have intended that, so the Court invoked the Holy Trinity principle that a thing may be within the letter of a statute but not within its spirit. The legislative history confirmed the narrow reading: Executive Order 11007 was never applied to the ABA Committee, and the Conference Committee added "or utilized" without explanation while stating that the Act does not reach committees not directly established by or for agencies. Calling the question close, and noting the formidable Article II questions, the majority applied constitutional avoidance from Crowell v. Benson: where an otherwise acceptable construction raises serious constitutional problems, the Court adopts an alternative unless plainly contrary to congressional intent. Kennedy, concurring in the judgment, differed on method: the plain language covers the committee, the absurdity exception requires a patently absurd result, and courts should not search legislative history for a spirit; he would have held FACA unconstitutional as applied.

topics.lrs-s-avoidance: The majority treats avoidance as decisive: with the text and history in equipoise, the Court adopts the reading that keeps FACA away from the President's Article II nomination power.
topics.lrs-k-absurdity: Brennan rejects the literal reading of "utilized" because it would reach consultations with the NAACP, an American Legion post or a political party; Kennedy answers that none of that is patently absurd.
topics.lrs-k-legislative-history: The Court relies on Executive Order 11007, the Conference Report and the unexplained insertion of "or utilized" to narrow the word, while Kennedy calls the account one-sided and unauthoritative.
topics.lrs-k-purposivism: The majority follows Holy Trinity, holding that the ABA Committee is within the letter of FACA but not within its spirit as revealed by the statute's purposes.
topics.lrs-k-textualism: Kennedy's concurrence argues that the plain language should be the starting and stopping point and that reading in a narrower meaning amends the statute by judicial interpretation.

learning.separateOpinions: Justice Brennan wrote for five Justices (White, Marshall, Blackmun and Stevens joined). Justice Kennedy, joined by Chief Justice Rehnquist and Justice O'Connor, concurred in the judgment only: the plain meaning of "utilized" covers the ABA Committee, the absurdity exception is confined to results Congress could not possibly have intended, and the majority's Holy Trinity method amends the statute by interpretation; he would have reached the constitutional question and held FACA unconstitutional as applied to the President's nomination of judges. Justice Scalia took no part. The judgment was 8 to 0; the statutory reasoning was 5 to 3.
learning.why: The case teaches the constitutional avoidance canon as a tiebreaker when text and legislative history are in tension, and the absurdity doctrine in its Holy Trinity form; Kennedy's concurrence supplies the textualist objection that avoidance and absurdity apply only where the text is ambiguous or the result patently absurd.
